questions.question: What is a monopoly?
questions.expected_answer: A monopoly is a market in which one firm produces all of the output.
questions.evidence_quote: In the case of monopoly, one firm produces all of the output in a market.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: monopoly a situation in which one firm produces all of the output in a market

questions.question: What are barriers to entry?
questions.expected_answer: Barriers to entry are the legal, technological, or market forces that discourage or prevent potential competitors from entering a market.
questions.evidence_quote: Barriers to entry are the legal, technological, or market forces that discourage or prevent potential competitors from entering a market.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: barriers to entry the legal, technological, or market forces that may discourage or prevent potential competitors from entering a market

questions.question: What conditions lead to a natural monopoly?
questions.expected_answer: A natural monopoly arises when economies of scale are large relative to the quantity demanded in the market.
questions.evidence_quote: Economists call this situation, when economies of scale are large relative to the quantity demanded in the market, a natural monopoly.

questions.question: In section 9.1, why were other firms unable to compete with ALCOA in aluminum in the 1930s?
questions.expected_answer: ALCOA controlled most of the supply of bauxite, so other firms could not produce enough aluminum to compete.
questions.evidence_quote: Back in the 1930s, when ALCOA controlled most of the bauxite, other firms were simply unable to produce enough aluminum to compete.

questions.question: What do governments do to create a legal monopoly?
questions.expected_answer: The government erects barriers to entry by prohibiting or limiting competition.
questions.evidence_quote: For some products, the government erects barriers to entry by prohibiting or limiting competition.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: legal monopoly legal prohibitions against competition, such as regulated monopolies and intellectual property protection

questions.question: How do patents let innovative firms recover their research and development costs?
questions.expected_answer: Patents give limited monopoly power so that firms can recoup their R&D investment before other firms can produce the product more cheaply.
questions.evidence_quote: The idea is to provide limited monopoly power so that innovative firms can recoup their investment in R&D, but then to allow other firms to produce the product more cheaply once the patent expires.

questions.question: What is predatory pricing?
questions.expected_answer: Predatory pricing is when a firm uses the threat of sharp price cuts to discourage competition.
questions.evidence_quote: One method is known as predatory pricing, in which a firm uses the threat of sharp price cuts to discourage competition.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: predatory pricing when an existing firm uses sharp but temporary price cuts to discourage new competition

questions.question: What demand curve does a monopolist face?
questions.expected_answer: The market demand curve, which is downward-sloping.
questions.evidence_quote: its demand curve is the same as the market demand curve, which is, unlike that for a perfectly competitive firm, downward-sloping

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: A monopolist perceives the demand curve that it faces to be the same as the market demand curve

questions.question: Why does total revenue for a monopolist first rise and then fall as it sells more output?
questions.expected_answer: To sell more output the monopolist must cut its price; selling more raises revenue but the lower price reduces it.
questions.evidence_quote: Selling more output raises revenue, but lowering price reduces it.

questions.question: Why is a monopolist's marginal revenue less than the price of the unit it sells?
questions.expected_answer: Because the lower price applies to all units sold, so marginal revenue is less than the price of that unit.
questions.evidence_quote: Because of the lower price on all units sold, the marginal revenue of selling a unit is less than the price of that unit

questions.question: In section 9.2, what rule does a profit-maximizing monopoly follow to choose its quantity of output?
questions.expected_answer: Produce up to the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC).
questions.evidence_quote: a profit-maximizing monopoly should follow the rule of producing up to the quantity where marginal revenue is equal to marginal cost

questions.question: Once a monopolist has chosen its output, how does it decide what price to charge?
questions.expected_answer: It charges what the market is willing to pay, read from the demand curve at the chosen quantity.
questions.evidence_quote: The monopolist will charge what the market is willing to pay.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: charge the price for that quantity of output as determined by the market demand curve

questions.question: Why is a monopoly considered allocatively inefficient?
questions.expected_answer: Monopolies do not supply enough output to be allocatively efficient.
questions.evidence_quote: what economists object to is that monopolies do not supply enough output to be allocatively efficient

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: Monopolists are not allocatively efficient, because they do not produce at the quantity where P = MC.

questions.question: In what ways can a firm make its products different from those of its competitors?
questions.expected_answer: Through physical aspects, location, intangible aspects, and perceptions of the product.
questions.evidence_quote: A firm can try to make its products different from those of its competitors in several ways: physical aspects of the product, location from which it sells the product, intangible aspects of the product, and perceptions of the product.

questions.question: What characterizes monopolistic competition?
questions.expected_answer: Many firms compete against each other but sell products that are distinctive in some way.
questions.evidence_quote: Monopolistic competition involves many firms competing against each other, but selling products that are distinctive in some way.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: monopolistic competition many firms competing to sell similar but differentiated products

questions.question: How does the demand curve facing a monopolistically competitive firm compare with that of a monopoly in terms of elasticity?
questions.expected_answer: It is more elastic than a monopoly's because there are substitutes.
questions.evidence_quote: Since there are substitutes, the demand curve facing a monopolistically competitive firm is more elastic than that of a monopoly where there are no close substitutes.

questions.question: In section 10.1, what happens to monopolistically competitive firms' economic profits in the long run?
questions.expected_answer: Entry and exit drive them toward zero economic profit.
questions.evidence_quote: in the long run, entry and exit will drive these firms toward a zero economic profit outcome

questions.question: How can a successful advertising campaign help a monopolistically competitive firm?
questions.expected_answer: It may let the firm sell a greater quantity, charge a higher price, or both.
questions.evidence_quote: a successful advertising campaign may allow a firm to sell either a greater quantity or to charge a higher price, or both

questions.question: What defines an oligopoly?
questions.expected_answer: A small number of large firms have all or most of the sales in an industry.
questions.evidence_quote: Oligopoly arises when a small number of large firms have all or most of the sales in an industry.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: oligopoly when a few large firms have all or most of the sales in an industry

questions.question: What does mutual interdependence mean in an oligopoly?
questions.expected_answer: Decisions such as output, price, and advertising depend on the decisions of other firms.
questions.evidence_quote: We typically characterize oligopolies by mutual interdependence where various decisions such as output, price, and advertising depend on other

questions.question: How can the relationship between market demand and economies of scale limit an oligopoly to only a few firms?
questions.expected_answer: Market quantity demanded may be only two or three times the quantity needed to reach minimum average cost, leaving room for only two or three firms.
questions.evidence_quote: Quantity demanded in the market may also be two or three times the quantity needed to produce at the minimum of the average cost curve

questions.question: In section 10.2, what is a cartel?
questions.expected_answer: A group of firms with a formal agreement to collude to produce the monopoly output and sell at the monopoly price.
questions.evidence_quote: A group of firms that have a formal agreement to collude to produce the monopoly output and sell at the monopoly price is called a cartel.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: cartel a group of firms that collude to produce the monopoly output and sell at the monopoly price

questions.question: What is game theory?
questions.expected_answer: A branch of mathematics that analyzes situations in which players make decisions and receive payoffs based on what other players decide.
questions.evidence_quote: economists use game theory, a branch of mathematics that analyzes situations in which players must make decisions and then receive payoffs based on what other players decide to do

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: game theory a branch of mathematics that economists use to analyze situations in which players must make decisions and then receive payoffs based on what decisions the other players make

questions.question: What did the British Tea Act make the East India Company in the American colonies?
questions.expected_answer: The sole legal supplier of tea to the American colonies.
questions.evidence_quote: The act continued the tax on teas and made the East India Company the sole legal supplier of tea to the American colonies.

questions.question: What is the key difference between marginal revenue for a perfectly competitive firm and for a monopolist?
questions.expected_answer: Under perfect competition marginal revenue equals price; for a monopolist it does not, because changes in output affect the price.
questions.evidence_quote: in the case of perfect competition, marginal revenue is equal to price (MR = P), while for a monopolist, marginal revenue is not equal to the price

questions.question: In section 9.1, why can one producer serve the market more efficiently than several smaller natural-monopoly utilities?
questions.expected_answer: Because of economies of scale, one producer avoids the duplicate physical capital investments that smaller producers would need.
questions.evidence_quote: because of economies of scale, one producer can serve the entire market more efficiently than a number of smaller producers that would need to make duplicate physical capital investments

questions.question: What happens to a firm's quantity demanded at a given price as more firms enter a monopolistically competitive market?
questions.expected_answer: The quantity demanded for any particular firm declines.
questions.evidence_quote: As more firms enter the market, the quantity demanded at a given price for any particular firm will decline

questions.question: What two conflicting temptations do oligopolistic firms face?
questions.expected_answer: To collaborate as if they were a single monopoly, or to compete individually by expanding output and cutting prices.
questions.evidence_quote: which face two conflicting temptations: to collaborate as if they were a single monopoly, or to individually compete to gain profits by expanding output levels and cutting prices

questions.question: Why did the soap cartel disintegrate?
questions.expected_answer: Because of the strong temptation for each member to maximize its own individual profits.
questions.evidence_quote: Like many cartels, the soap cartel disintegrated due to the very strong temptation for each member to maximize its own individual profits.

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: each individual oligopoly faces a private temptation to produce just a slightly higher quantity and earn slightly higher profit

questions.question: In section 10.2, what is a kinked demand curve?
questions.expected_answer: A demand curve in which competing oligopoly firms commit to match price cuts but not price increases.
questions.evidence_quote: the kinked demand curve, in which competing oligopoly firms commit to match price cuts, but not price increases

alternative_gold_evidence.quote: kinked demand curve a perceived demand curve that arises when competing oligopoly firms commit to match price cuts, but not price increases
